## Abstract

We study how financialization changed the informativeness of drivers for commodity futures returns. Based on a broad set of commodity futures, we show that the predictive power of fundamental, financial, and uncertainty variables for commodity returns varies substantially across different stages of financialization. We relate the changing informativeness of the drivers to the presence of financial hedgers, who use commodity exposure for portfolio diversification. Using the highly financialized crude oil market as a laboratory, we find that when the market share of financial hedgers is high, the predictive power of financial variables for short-term commodity returns increases, while the informativeness of fundamental variables for longer-term returns declines.

## 1. Introduction

Since the early 2000s, a new group of financial investors, so-called financial hedgers, have entered commodity futures markets, leading to the “financialization” of commodities. In this study, we examine how financialization and the presence of financial hedgers relate to the informativeness of drivers for commodity futures returns. Understanding what drives commodity futures returns enhances the precision of market research outlooks, aids commercial traders in refining their hedging strategies, and helps financial traders to make better investment decisions.

We demonstrate that the lead–lag relationships between commodities and their return drivers, such as real activity and stock market returns, change throughout distinct stages of financialization. 
We begin our analysis by examining 21 potential common return drivers across 35 commodity futures. Commodity returns primarily reflect news about future cash flows (Han et al., 2025). We focus on three groups of drivers that simultaneously affect the cash flow expectations across a broad range of different commodities. Firstly, commodity prices react to changes in macroeconomic fundamentals that shift (expected) aggregate supply and demand (Pindyck and Rotemberg, 1990, Barsky and Kilian, 2001). Secondly, the financialization led to a tighter connection between commodity and equity markets (e.g., Büyükşahin and Robe, 2014, Basak and Pavlova, 2016). Lastly, uncertainty affects commodity prices through both fundamental and financial channels, such as speculation, delayed investment, and precautionary demand (Kilian, 2009, Cheng and Xiong, 2014). We distinguish between daily and monthly return drivers due to heterogeneous investment and hedging horizons. We estimate the lead–lag relationships between commodity returns and their drivers using Granger causality tests based on vector autoregressive (VAR) models. Since many macroeconomic indicators are only available at monthly frequency, we use Granger causality tests based on mixed-frequency (MF-)VAR models whenever driver variables are not observed daily (Ghysels, 2016, Ghysels et al., 2016).

Because research claims that financialization fundamentally changed the behavior of commodity markets (e.g., Cheng and Xiong, 2014), we run subsample analyses over three distinct stages of the financialization: pre-financialization (1996–2003), financialization (2004–2013), and the debatable process of de-financialization (2014–2022).^{1} We do not find common return drivers across different types of commodities in the pre-financialization period. Consistent with research showing that co-movement among commodities and between commodities and stock markets increased with the financialization, we find stock market returns, implied volatility, and investor risk aversion to predict the returns of the majority of commodities in the period from 2004 to 2013. Although our results indicate that commodity prices contain information from daily stock returns, monthly real activity, and macroeconomic uncertainty contribute further valuable information for longer-run futures returns that is not captured by stock markets alone. Using data after 2013, we cannot confirm many of the short-term Granger-causal relationships with stock market returns. Moreover, we find substantially fewer long-term Granger causalities from fundamental variables but more from macroeconomic uncertainty compared to the financialization sample. Overall, our results suggest that commodity returns became less sensitive to financial variables compared to the main period of the financialization.

As more financial hedgers trade in commodity markets, we argue that financial variables will become more valuable for predicting commodity returns, while the predictive power of fundamental variables will decline.

We use crude oil as an example of a strongly financialized commodity to study our hypothesis. We measure the informativeness of the driver variables for future oil returns by the drivers’ ability to improve purely autoregressive return forecasts. We define this excess predictability as the difference in out-of-sample prediction errors of a driver-augmented VAR model and an autoregressive model that does not use information from the driver variables. Then, we analyze whether the presence of financial hedgers predicts excess predictability, while controlling for economic activity, macroeconomic uncertainty, stock market volatility, and inventory levels. To proxy financial hedger presence, we use the Hamilton and Wu (2014) risk premium defined as the difference between the rationally expected and the observed futures price. ## 2. Data

### 2.1. Commodity futures

We collect daily settlement prices of 35 commodity futures via Bloomberg from January 1996 to June 2022. Our data set covers a wide range of agricultural and energy commodities as well as industrial and precious metals. Table 1 presents summary statistics for daily log returns calculated as: (1){r}_{t}=100\times ln\left({F}_{i,t}/{F}_{i,t-1}\right),where {F}_{i,t} denotes the daily settlement price (in USD) of the nearest contract i on trading day t that has at least 15 calendar days to expiration. We construct the continuous return series using settlement prices of Bloomberg’s generic front and second contract. Additionally, we construct equally-weighted portfolios for each group of commodities. We also extract a common return factor, defined as the first principal component (PC) of daily log returns across 31 commodities for which data are available from August 1997 onward, when industrial metals price data become available. We provide a time series plot of the common return factor, factor loadings, and correlations to all commodities in the online appendix. Considering the full sample, the common factor captures 23% of total commodity return variation, whereas its correlation is highest with Brent crude oil (0.81) and lowest with feeder cattle (0.07).


### 2.2. Potential common return drivers of commodity futures

Motivated by theory and empirical findings of previous studies, we select 21 fundamental, financial, and uncertainty variables – as listed in Table 2 – that we consider ex ante as potential common drivers of commodity futures returns. More detailed descriptions and data sources are summarized in the online appendix.

Our set of fundamental variables primarily encompasses indicators of global real economic activity. Shocks to real activity indicate changes in the aggregate demand for commodities. Findings of Barsky and Kilian (2001), Kilian (2009), and more recent work by Alquist et al. (2020), Hollstein et al. (2021), and Delle Chiaie et al. (2022) suggest that aggregate economic activity is a primary driver of commodity price fluctuations. Table 2. Potential drivers of commodity futures returns.

## 5. Conclusion

In this study, we examine how financialization has altered the informativeness of return drivers in commodity futures markets. We find that the periods before and after the onset of financialization differ in the variables that predict commodity returns. Our findings for the crude oil market suggest that the growing presence of financial hedgers is associated with a decline in the informativeness of fundamental variables, such as real activity, for long-term returns. By contrast, financial variables, including stock market returns, volatility, and the risk aversion of financial investors, become more important predictors of short-term commodity returns when the presence of financial hedgers using commodities for portfolio diversification is high.

# Publication in the Journal of Banking and Finance

© Elsevier

Tom Dudda (Doctoral Candidate at the Chair of Finance and Financial Technology) and Thomas Walther (Utrecht University and Research Fellow at the Chair of Finance and Financial Technology) published their article titled “Financialization and the Drivers of Commodity Futures Returns” together with Duc K. Nguyen and Tony Klein in the Journal of Banking and Finance.

Their study investigates how the informativeness of return drivers in commodity futures markets changes with the presence of so-called financial hedgers. Financial hedgers gain commodity exposure to diversify their investment portfolios. As such, their commodity investments mainly depend on their risk-bearing capacity and the performance of other portfolio assets (e.g., stocks) rather than on commodity market fundamentals.

The authors arrive at two interesting findings. First, the predictive power of commodity return drivers changes across distinct stages of the financialization of commodity markets. Second, they use the highly financialized crude oil market to show that when the market share of financial hedgers is high, the predictive power of financial variables (e.g., stock returns) for short-term commodity returns increases. In contrast, the informativeness of fundamental variables (e.g., real activity) for longer-term returns declines.
